name: Party list extractor and conflict-check builder for litigation paralegals
pain: Paralegals retype dozens of named parties from scanned complaints into case management software so conflict checks can run. New solo and appearance attorneys keep conflict databases in homemade spreadsheets.
who_pays: Litigation paralegals at small firms using Clio or similar; solo and freelance appearance attorneys
pay_signal: Moderate. [39] already pays for Clio, faces an end-of-day deadline for 54 defendants and asks for a tool. [48] is hand-building a conflict spreadsheet to manage malpractice risk. [36] is a builder probing demand, not buyer evidence.
product_idea: Web tool: upload a complaint or docket PDF (scanned is fine), Claude API pulls out parties, roles, counsel and entity types, cleans and dedupes the names, then exports a Clio-ready contact CSV. An optional conflict-check sheet in Google Sheets fuzzy-matches new parties against the firm's past list. Assets: Claude API (near-zero cost for OCR'd text reasoning) and Google Sheets API.
known_competitors: Clio's own AI features, CoCounsel/Thomson Reuters, Docketbird, generic PDF-to-Excel OCR tools; none appear focused on party-list import
check_next: Search r/paralegal and Clio forums for 'import parties' or 'conflict check' threads. Confirm Clio's contact CSV import format. Offer a free 10-page trial to 20 paralegals.

crowding.reason: Conflict checking is crowded (Clio built-in, Client Conflict Check $199/yr, ConflictCheck from $49/mo), and TackleAI already extracts parties from scanned pleadings to CSV; no proof yet that anyone pays for extraction by itself.

pay_proof.claim: Client Conflict Check charges solo firms $199/year (30-day free trial)
ConflictCheck sells conflict screening to solo/small firms at $49, $119 or $249 per month
Clio's AI deadline extraction from court documents is limited to the Core plan and above (paid tier)
Small firms pay for party extraction from complaints specifically

name: Givebutter-to-acknowledgment letter and household merge tool

name: Fair housing language checker for listing copy
pain: Agents and brokers write rental and sale listings with phrases that violate fair housing rules (neighborhood characterizations, family or ability language). Compliance review is done by manually reading listings.
who_pays: Listing agents, rental brokers, broker compliance managers
pay_signal: Weak to moderate. Only one post, [66], but it comes from a 15-year professional manually auditing NYC listings who found high violation rates. Fair housing violations carry fines, giving clear liability motivation.
product_idea: Browser extension that runs on MLS, StreetEasy and Zillow listing-entry forms. It flags risky phrases with an explanation and a compliant rewrite using Claude API plus a curated rule list (federal, NYC, CA protected classes). A broker plan adds batch audit of exported listings. Assets: Claude API; HyperFrames/YouTube for short 'phrase of the week' marketing videos; SEO content tooling.
known_competitors: Some AI listing writers include fair housing filters (ListingAI, Epique, some MLS-built checkers); free word lists from Realtor associations
check_next: Test whether existing MLS input screens already block phrases in NYC, CA and TX. Interview 5 brokerage compliance managers. Check Chrome Web Store for existing fair housing extensions.

crowding.reason: Several free fair housing listing checkers, MLS-built remarks checks, a paid Chrome extension and AI listing writers ($19-$36/mo) already flag and rewrite risky phrases; no evidence that a standalone checker can charge.
